# Fixing Seized Calipers: When to Replace One Side vs. Both

Replacing brake components on a single axle is often treated as an all-or-nothing proposition, similar to how tires or rotors are swapped in pairs. However, the mechanics of caliper maintenance differ significantly from rolling resistance issues. While you might replace front brakes simultaneously due to uneven wear rates affecting safety margins, addressing a seized slide pin requires a different diagnostic mindset.

The core issue described here involves the guide pins (slide bearings) locking up, causing the caliper piston to drag against the rotor even when the parking brake is disengaged. In your Kia Picanto BA 2008 case, replacing the journals temporarily resolved the friction because you restored the necessary clearance for lateral movement. The recurrence of overheating and high-speed noise suggests the new pins are either wearing again due to improper lubrication or that the caliper housing itself has developed scoring or corrosion at the contact points.

When deciding whether to replace just the affected caliper or swap both, consider the mechanical symmetry of hydraulic systems. Unlike tires, where rolling resistance differences can cause handling imbalances, brake drag creates thermal stress primarily on one side. However, if the root cause is environmental exposure—such as water ingress into the dust boot leading to corrosion—it is statistically probable that the opposite caliper is also compromised, even if it hasn't seized yet.

In many modern vehicles, including older compact cars like your Picanto, calipers are often manufactured as single, solid units without serviceable inner guide pins. This design choice reduces part count but complicates maintenance. If you have already extracted and replaced the journals once, attempting a second extraction carries a high risk of stripping the threads in the housing or damaging the seal bore. Once that threshold is crossed, the cost-benefit analysis shifts heavily toward replacement.

Financially, replacing one caliper for €100 versus rebuilding it with new pins for €17 hinges on long-term reliability. If the noise fluctuates between 120 km/h and 140 km/h, this indicates intermittent drag that only manifests under specific thermal conditions. This inconsistency often points to a warped rotor or uneven pad thickness, but given your history of seized pins, the caliper is likely the culprit.

If you choose to replace only one unit, inspect the opposite caliper meticulously during disassembly. Look for rust on the slide pin holes and check if the dust boots are intact. If the housing shows signs of corrosion or if the pins are stiff upon removal, installing a new caliper on one side while keeping a degraded one creates an imbalance in braking torque distribution. This can lead to premature wear on the new pads or uneven rotor wear patterns over time.

For a vehicle at 100,000 km with four-year-old front brakes, proactive replacement of both units is often the most cost-effective strategy to prevent future labor costs associated with extracting seized components again. The slight price difference between buying two used calipers versus one, combined with the peace of mind from eliminating potential drag on the passenger side, usually outweighs the marginal savings of keeping a suspect unit in service.

Always ensure that new guide pins are packed with high-temperature brake grease before reassembly. Using standard lithium grease can lead to degradation under braking heat, causing the very seizure problem you are trying to solve. Additionally, verify that the caliper piston seals have been properly lubricated and seated to prevent binding during the initial break-in period.
